to make repairs. As a result, on April 3, 2018 an employee sustained serious
injury from an explosion that occurred while he made repairs with the use of

On April 11, 2019, an employee was working for a manufacturer of miscellaneous
wood products. He was sharpening knives to replace dull knives in a wood
chipper. He was adjacent to the site's smaller chipper. He noticed that the
conveyor leading to the chipper was backing up with wood chips (which indicated
a blockage in the chipper). The employee reached into the small chipper with his
right hand to remove the blockage. As he did this, he slipped on the working
surface he was standing on. His right arm moved forward and down into the
chipper. The middle finger on his right hand came into contact with the moving
knives. He sustained an amputation of the tip of his right middle finger. He was
hospitalized.
At 3:09 p.m. on April 10, 2019, Employee #1, employed by a resort hotel, was
tasked with replacing skylights and metal roof panels on the roof of a one-story
horse stable.  As the employee removed an existing roof panel below a skylight,
an unsupported piece of foam board was exposed.  The employee stepped onto the
foam board and fell into the stable, a fall height of 13 feet.  The employee was
not using any fall protection.  Emergency services responded, and the employee
was evacuated by air to the hospital.  He was admitted and treated for a
fractured pelvis, multiple fractured ribs, and fractures to the spine.

The tractor and tanks were at the intersection of two roads, when the anhydrous

looking for a fog nozzle. Due to the leak, there was a release of gas that sent

At 2:00 p.m. on May 1, 2019, Employee #1 and a coworker, employed by a
construction company, were digging by hand a trench in Type C soil outside a
multifamily residential structure in preparation to install new piping.  The
trench measured 8 feet deep, 13 feet long, and 18 inches wide.  The trench wall
collapsed, trapping both employees.  Emergency services responded.  Employee #1,
whose legs had been pinned by the soil and rock, was transported to the
hospital, where he was admitted for treatment of contusions and lacerations.
His coworker did not require medical treatment.
At approximately 5:00 p.m. on April 19, 2019, an employee walked upstairs from a
PLC control area to a mezzanine level, prepared to take an ingredient sample
from a maltodextrin radial feeder. The employee had to rotate a spindle cover
180 degrees from top-to-bottom to access an opening in a maltodextrin feeder
which would facilitate sample-depositing into a large plastic bag. As the
employee performed this challenging task due to her short stature, the thumb of
a glove was caught by a slow-moving rotating spindle, causing a partial
amputation. The in-running nip point was not guarded. The opening was
approximately 4 in. wide by 12 in. long. The employee was hospitalized for these
injuries.
At approximately 6:30 p.m. on April 24, 2019, an employee was preparing a 1:1
HNO3 in a 1000ml flask in a fume hood. The employee was working in a laboratory
and poured a 1:1 HNO3 (nitric acid) out of a 1000ml flask into a 4-liter reagent
bottle inside a fume hood.  While transferring the 1:1 NHO3 into the 4-liter
reagent bottle, the neck of the 1000ml flask broke splashing HNO3 onto the
employee's chest and face resulting in chemical burns to the chest and face. The
employee sustained chemical burns to the chest and face and was transported to
the emergency room for treatment for burns and kept for observation due to
possible inhalation of nitric acid.
At 10:30 a.m. on April 29, 2019, an employee was working as a laborer for a farm
management service. He had dropped off a trailer that contained bins of lettuce
in a produce yard. As he was walking in the yard, he was struck by a rough
terrain forklift that was backing up. He was struck in his right leg. He
suffered a fracture to his right leg. His supervisor transported him to a clinic
by his supervisor. The employee was subsequently transferred by ambulance to a
medical center in Salinas, CA. He was admitted, and he remained there for
treatment until May 5, 2019. The Division was notified of the incident at
approximately 7:55 p.m. on April 29, 2019.
At 8:00 a.m. on April 24, 2019, Employee #1, employed by a masonry contractor,
was operating a forklift at the construction site of a new commercial building.
He reached under the lift's boom to remove shovels, which involved standing up
from the seat of the cab and leaning out the front window to grab the shovels.
The employee's hip struck against the lift's boom control, and the boom lowered
and struck his right hand, amputating the ring and pinky fingers.  The employee
was transported to the hospital, where he was admitted for treatment of the
amputations.
At approximately 1:30 p.m. on April 26, 2019, an employee was working for a
wholesaler of recyclable materials. He was working as an inspector. His job was
to direct the drivers of trucks coming into the yard where to dump material. The
material had to be dumped in certain areas, depending on the type of material it
was. The employee was also directing the operators of excavators, who picked up
the material after it had been dumped and placed it on railroad cars. On the day
of the incident, the employee was standing behind a truck to direct the driver
clothing, eye protection, and gloves; however, he was hospitalized with several
burns to his hands and face.
At 10:00 a.m. on November 7, 2018, Employee #1 and several coworkers were
flagging a vehicle operator when he was caught and pinned between two trucks.
The employee was transported to the hospital for treatment of a fractured
pelvis.
At 7:00 a.m. on April 22, 2019, Employee #1, employed by a poultry processing
facility, was operating the combo dumper. Employee #1 went down the stairs to
unhook a cylinder airline without locking and tagging the combo dumper out. His
left index finger was caught between the cylinders and amputated at the first
joint. Employee #1 was hospitalized.
On April 12, 2019, an employee is caught between some equipment and was killed.
No further details were provided by the initial report.
At 2:30 p.m. on April 16, 2019, Employee #1, employed by a candy manufacturer,
was placing a plastic bag over the motor of a mixer. The equipment was running
and Employee # 1 performing the cleaning cycle. His fingers were caught in the
rotating belts and pulley. Employee #1 received amputation injuries to the
fingers on his right hand including but not limited to his index, middle, ring,
and pinky fingers. He was hospitalized.
At 10:45 a.m. on April 17, 2019, Employee #1, employed by an aluminum and steel
component fabricator, was in the warehouse checking on shipping materials. While
he was checking the shipping materials, a coworker driving a lift truck, backed
up over Employee #1's foot. Employee #1's foot was broken. He was hospitalized.
At 3:00 p.m. on April 22, 2019, Employee #1, employed by a metal finishing
company, was removing a hoist that held up a hinged, scissor-like, lifting
device. He did not lockout the system. He stood on the lifting device as he was
working on the hoist. The hoist supported the lifting device. Employee #1
disconnected the hoist from the lifting device. The lifting device closed and
his feet were crushed in the scissor-like action of the device. Employee #1's
feet were crushed, and he was hospitalized to treat the  fractures in his feet.
His toes were also amputated.
At 11:30 a.m. on April 18, 2019, Employee #1, employed by a bulk handling
equipment manufacturing company, was moving a 120 inch by 60 inch sheet of ?
inch thick carbon steel onto a plasma table while the table was operating. There
are two conflicting reports. One is that, as the plate was transferred to the

crane and it pinched Employee #1's right middle finger between the plate and the
table grating. The second report is that the plate struck an emergency stop
(E-stop) cable and then swung down pinching Employee #1's fingertip between the
table grating and the steel plate. His right middle fingertip was amputated.
Hospitalization was not required.
At 3:30 p.m. on March 15, 2019, Employee #1, employed by a trailer manufacturing
company, was using an electric Sawzall to cut his way out of a restroom trailer.
He had just finished applying a flammable adhesive to the wallboard in the
trailer. There was not adequate ventilation for the flammable adhesive vapors in
the trailer so an explosion occurred during cutting. Employee #1 received burns
to his hands, arms, and face from the flash explosion. He was hospitalized.
At 9:00 a.m. on April 11, 2019, Employee #1, employed by a department store, was
getting ready to open the front doors of the store. A gust of wind hit the front
doors as the employee was opening them, and the doors struck her in the head.
She had a concussion and was hospitalized.
At 6:10 a.m. on April 19, 2019, an employee was performing service work on a
baler. The Balemaster (Model:  44750-10, G, J, J, 4, Q, T, U, X, Z, 7, Z, 9;
Serial Number:  B1022-04-13389583) had five swords which became lodge in a bale
while attempting to pull wire through to tie the bale at the end of the process.
A third shift maintenance coworker began working on the baler and successfully
removed the swords before handing it to his maintenance supervisor at
approximately 5:40 a.m.  The maintenance supervisor assessed the piece of
equipment and began servicing it without performing lockout/tagout.  The
maintenance supervisor made a jig with a flexible conduit tube and metal hook
taped with electrical tape.  At approximately 6:00 a.m., the employee assisted
in retrieving the metal hook on the opposite of the baler from the maintenance
supervisor. The employee did not perform lockout/tagout prior to placing his
hand in the danger zone.  As the flex tube and metal hook went through the
opening, it broke. The maintenance supervisor decided another approach would be
needed, discussed it with the employee and then walked away. The maintenance
supervisor observed product piling up in the chute leading to the baler and
decided to reverse the ram in order to empty the chute. The maintenance
supervisor was not able to see the other side of the baler when he was at the
controls. While reversing the ram, the employee's hand was in an opening in an
attempt to reach the wire. The employee's hand was severed from the ram and end
of equipment. The employee yelled and was provided with medical treatment from
designated first responders followed by local EMTs, where he was transported to
the hospital.
At 11:30 a.m. on April 22, 2019, an employee was insulating some pipe and fell
from through the false ceiling on the mezzanine.  The employee fell over 9 feet
before striking the floor with his head and was killed.
On December 13, 2018, Employee #1 was performing electrical work at the
construction site of a power plant.  As he stepped into the generator circuit
breaker box to perform brain work, he made contact with an energized circuit.
The employee sustained an electric shock.  He was transported to the hospital
and admitted for treatment.
At 10:00 a.m. on April 22, 2019, an employee was attempting to stop a pumping

At 9:30 a.m. on April 30, 2019, an employee was removing a plate clamp from a
steel plate. The clamp slipped, and the employee fell back and was killed from a

At 8:30 a.m. on May 1, 2019, an employee was working for a trucking and logging
firm. He was constructing a logging spur road. He was operating a Caterpillar
D6C bulldozer, with serial number 76A-3570, to make room to set up a yarder. As
he pushed brush over the road edge, he lost control of the bulldozer. It went
over the ridge and travelled approximately 90 meters (300 feet) down the ridge.
It came to rest against some trees. The employee was found by coworkers outside
the cab in the vicinity of the bulldozer. He had not been wearing his seat belt.
He suffered fractures, in the form of a broken arm, a broken back, and broken
ribs. He was hospitalized.
At 7:30 a.m. on Saturday, May 4, 2019, Employee #1, a 70-year-old employee, was
working for a firm that managed and operated parking lots and garages. He was
working as a valet parking attendant at a parking garage for an upscale hotel.
It was his first day on the job, and it was the first time that he had observed
a manlift. He had arrived at the worksite at approximately 6:45 a.m. He went to
the bathroom and asked a regular worker if he could see the other levels. The
manlift was used to transport workers vertically from floor to floor inside the
building. It was an endless power-driven belt with steps and handholds that
moved in one direction. The employee was on the ground floor. As he was
attempting to get on the step or platform (the passenger carrying unit) of the
manlift, he fell through the floor opening. He fell from the ground floor to the
lowest level of the garage. This was three levels or approximately 9 meters (30
feet). He was unconscious. Emergency medical workers transported him to Thomas
Jefferson University Hospital. He was hospitalized. Medical personnel placed 29
surgical staples into the top of his head. This was a multi-employer worksite.
There were two inspection reports generated for this investigation. Inspection
1440966 was for the hotel. Inspection 1398705 was for operator of the parking
lots and garages.
At noon on January 8, 2019, an employee was working for a municipal government's
department of public health. He was working at a mental health facility. He was
assisting a client who used a wheelchair into a company van. The employee
assisted the client inside the van. As he returned the wheelchair to the back of

curb. He suffered head and neck trauma. He was hospitalized.
At 10:00 a.m. on April 26, 2019, an employee was working for a merchant
wholesaler of roofing, siding, and insulation material. The firm sold supplies

the equipment to speak with a supervisor. As he was talking to the supervisor,
his forklift rolled forwarded. The employee was pinned and crushed between his
forklift and the supervisor's parked forklift. He suffered a fractured pelvis.
He was hospitalized.
At 5:30 a.m. on May 4, 2019, an employee was working for a firm that

At 12:00 p.m. on April 19, 2019, Employee #1 and Employee #2 were observing a

At 2:30 p.m. on April 22, 2019, Employee #1 and a coworker, employed by a

the crossbeam.  The boom backed into and struck against the beam on which
Employee was working and to which he was tied off.  The beam fell, and Employee
#1 fell with it, a fall height of 15 feet.  Employee #1 was killed.
At 2:32 p.m. on April 23, 2019, an employee was killed while troubleshooting at

At 5:00 p.m. on March 20, 2019, Employee #1 was using an angel grinder to cut a

At 8:00 a.m. on April 12, 2019, an employee was installing fire sprinkler piping

unprotected balcony down 32 feet to the ground.  The employee fractured the
vertebrate and thumb and was hospitalized.
At 1:30 a.m. on April 23, 2019, an employee was checking and filling the pump
oil in the vacuum pump on top of the thermal forming press.  The employee opened
the fill cap on the vacuum pump located on top of the thermal forming press
while the pump was running.  Once the cap was opened, it sprayed hot
light-weight pump oil.  The employee was hospitalized with severe burns to the
chest.
At 10:30 a.m. on August 29, 2018, Employee #1, employed by a concrete
construction company, was engaged in construction of concrete parking
structures.  He was handling the rubber hose, 4-5 inches in diameter, that is
used to deliver concrete slurry from a concrete boom truck to the pour location.
As pumping resumed after a down time, there was a surge in the hose line as a
clog cleared, and the hose whipped violently due to the release of
energy/pressure that had built up.  The hose struck the employee on the left
side of his head, then whipped back and struck and fractured his right
clavicle/shoulder bone.  The employee was transported to the hospital and

At 7:19 p.m. on October 15, 2017, an employee and another worker were standing

explosion occurred in the test tank and a fire ensued. An employee sustained
burns, fractures, hearing loss, vision impairment, and foreign bodies in the
eye(s).
At 11:00 a.m. on March 28, 2019, an employee was walking to move a tree with his

supervisor immediately ran over and called for help from another coworker who

wing sections of a package sorting conveyor line to fold them into the storage
position. The employee had placed her finger in the pinch point on the frame

transported to Sharp Chula Vista Hospital and was admitted for treatment.

At 2:30 p.m. on April 30, 2019, an employee from a temporary employment agency
began his first day as a line worker for a firm that was engaged in millwork,
including flooring. He was a machine operator, and he worked on a press line. On
the line, he worked filling cracks and knot holes in floorboards before they
went through a planer. He was at a worksite, that of a firm that provided
general storage and warehousing. His employer, the millwork firm, was sharing
the building occupied by the storage and warehouse firm. The warehouse firm had
a Caterpillar model CG55KSTR powered industrial vehicle (PIV) that it used for
material handling operations. Warehouse employees operated it for some 2.5 hours
daily. It ran on liquid petroleum (LP). It was provided by an outside firm that
also performed maintenance. On April 30, 2019, the Caterpillar had fuel flow
issues that caused it to produce concentration levels of carbon monoxide (CO) in
excess of 50 ppm. After two or three hours, the millwork firm employee developed
a mild headache. Throughout the day, his headache grew so strong that when he
got home after work, he had his wife take him to the hospital. The hospital
analyzed his blood and transported him to a bigger hospital, for treatment of
elevated carboxyhemoglobin. He was hospitalized. From the analysis of the blood
drawn at the first hospital, it was calculated that the employee's 8-hour carbon
monoxide time weighted average exposure was 223.8 ppm. He had had been exposed
to 440 percent of the 8-hour time weighted average carbon monoxide exposure
limit of 50 ppm. On May 2, 2019, the PIV had an emissions test. The carbon
monoxide level in its exhaust was measured at 4.28 percent. Two other employees
at the site were exposed to carbon monoxide, but they were not hospitalized. An
OSHA inspector measured baseline CO level in the warehouse at 66 ppm. With the
doors closed and the PIVs operating, a lift truck firm employee measured the CO
level at 42,300 ppm.

manufactured rubber products for mechanical use. She was operating a Manhattan

machine guarding and the proper use of drilling machines. The employer took the
machine out of service. The employer has advised his staff to no longer hold

vise grips, instead. The employer also took the Grob vertical RWB #20856 bandsaw
out of service.
